title: Blended Malt Whisky Explained | Craft Beer School
desc: What blended malt whisky is, how it differs from single malt and blended Scotch and how to taste one with a sharper palate.
teaser: Blended malt is all malt whisky, from more than one distillery. It is not a lesser single malt.
standfirst: Blended malt sits between single malt and blended Scotch on the shelf and the name confuses plenty of people. It is whisky made only from malt, drawn from several distilleries. Here is what that means, why blenders make it and what to look for in the glass.
sections: All malt, more than one distillery

A blended malt is a mix of single malt whiskies from two or more distilleries. Every component is malt whisky: made from 100% malted barley and, in Scotland, distilled in pot stills. What it does not contain is grain whisky, the lighter column still spirit that makes up most of a standard blended Scotch.

So the word blended here refers to mixing distilleries, not mixing malt with grain. Our guide to malt, grain and blended whisky sets out the three families side by side. The quick version: single malt is one distillery and all malt, blended malt is many distilleries and all malt, blended whisky is malt plus grain.
The old names: vatted and pure malt

For decades the same style went by other names. Vatted malt was common, after the vats in which whiskies were mixed. Pure malt appeared on many labels too. Shoppers found both confusing and some thought pure malt meant single malt.

The Scotch Whisky Regulations 2009 settled it. In Scotland the legal category is now Blended Malt Scotch Whisky. The older terms may no longer be used on Scotch labels. Outside Scotland you may still see vatted malt or pure malt on older bottles or on whiskies from other countries, so read the back label.

A single distillery makes a spirit with its own fingerprint, shaped by its stills, yeast, fermentation time and cuts. A blender making a blended malt has a wider palette. They can take the fruit of one distillery, the weight of another and the smoke of a third, then build something none of them makes alone.

Consistency is the other reason. A blended malt drawn from many casks across several distilleries can taste the same year after year even when individual casks vary. That is the same skill that keeps a big blend steady, applied to malt only.

The rule for age statements is the same as for any Scotch: the number on the label is the age of the youngest whisky in the bottle. A 12 year old blended malt may contain much older whisky, but none younger than 12 years. Every component must also meet the Scotch minimum of three years in oak casks in Scotland and the bottle must be at least 40% ABV.

Many blended malts carry no age statement at all. That only means the blender chose not to state the youngest component. It tells you nothing either way about quality, so let the glass decide.

Pour about 25 ml into a tulip shaped glass. Nose it first without water, then add a few drops and nose again. With a blended malt, try to pick out the different strands rather than one single impression. Common notes include:

  • cereal, biscuit and malt from the barley
  • orchard fruit or tropical fruit from the spirit
  • vanilla and coconut from American oak
  • dried fruit and spice from sherry casks
  • smoke, if a peated malt is part of the recipe

Then taste, hold it on the tongue and notice how long the finish lasts. Keep a glass of water beside you and sip between pours. Tasting is about attention, not volume. Whisky is never part of an evening that ends with driving.
What the blender is actually doing

Building a blended malt starts with a target: a flavour the blender wants to hit batch after batch. They taste samples from dozens of casks, usually diluted to around 20% ABV so the nose does not tire. Each component gets a role. One malt might bring body, another lift, another a thread of smoke.

The components are then married. In practice that means mixing them and letting them rest together, often in a large vat or in casks, before reduction and bottling. Resting lets the different whiskies settle into one another. A blend bottled the day it was mixed can taste disjointed, with each malt still speaking on its own.

None of this is visible on the label. You taste the result of hundreds of small choices, which is why a well made blended malt often rewards slow attention more than a big single malt does.
Where blended malt fits in India

Indian shelves carry a mix of imported Scotch, Indian single malts and Indian blends. Blended malt is a good way to taste the house styles of several distilleries in one glass and work out which flavours you like. It also makes a fine comparison: taste a blended malt next to a single malt of similar age and see what the blender added and what the single distillery keeps.

Your first step: next time you pick up a whisky, read the back label and find the category. Single malt, blended malt or blended whisky. Then taste with that in mind.
faqs: Is blended malt the same as blended whisky?
No. Blended malt contains only malt whiskies from several distilleries. Blended whisky mixes malt whisky with grain whisky.
Is blended malt worse than single malt?
No. It is a different approach. Single malt shows one distillery, blended malt combines several to build a flavour none makes alone.
An older name for blended malt. Since the Scotch Whisky Regulations 2009, Scotch labels must use the term blended malt instead.
